headline: Patrick Stewart died at 86. He was Captain Picard.
summary: Patrick Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86 and had Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, which had never been made public. He spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company before Star Trek: The Next Generation made him Captain Picard for 178 episodes and four films. He was knighted in 2010.

cover_question.q: Was he a real spaceship captain?

cover_answer: No. He was an actor. He played one for 178 episodes.
table_question: Would you take a job everyone told you would flop?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: An actor called Patrick Stewart died on Wednesday at his home. He was 86, as old as a great-grandpa. On TV he was Captain Picard, who flew a spaceship called the Enterprise, but he was pretending, the way you pretend to be a pirate. He got to do his favourite thing for his whole long life.
5-7.why: Only if it comes up. A pretend captain, a very old man, his own home.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so if it comes up the feature is the pretend captain, a game they already play, and the death is a very old man at home. Cantor found the concrete and the near frighten this age; 86 and far away is neither. Expect "will you die?" Not for a very long time.

8-12.script: Patrick Stewart grew up in a Yorkshire house with no bathroom and memorised Shakespeare for fun. At 14 he learned Macbeth's speeches. After 14 years on stage he took a space show everyone said would flop. It ran 178 episodes, and when he played Macbeth 50 years on, the lines were still there.
8-12.why: Learned at 14, still there 50 years on. One chain.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out how effort becomes results, so the script runs one chain: a boy with no bathroom at home memorises Macbeth at 14, acts on stage for 14 years, takes the show everyone said would flop, and plays Macbeth 50 years on with the lines still there. Expect "did he get rich?" Yes. The show made him very wealthy.

13-17.script: Can a hard childhood make an actor? Patrick Stewart called the stage "a refuge from real life": his father beat his mother. He later wrote that violence "is always a choice a man makes." Second: he had dementia and nobody outside knew. Is a famous person owed that privacy?
13-17.why: A refuge made public, an illness kept private. Weigh both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a man who made the stage his refuge from a violent father and said so, and a man who kept his dementia private. The script asks which disclosures a public person owes, and they will test whether you argue honestly. Expect "would you tell people?" Say what you would do, and why.

5-7.q: Was he a real spaceship captain?
5-7.a: No. He was an actor who played one on TV. He liked it so much he did it for seven years and four films.

8-12.q: Why did everyone think Star Trek would flop?
8-12.a: A friend told him: get a suntan, make some money, go home.
His hair fell out as a teen. Star Trek's creator didn't mind.

13-17.q: Is a famous person owed privacy about illness?
13-17.a: His spokesperson said the diagnoses were never disclosed.
He did, in his memoir. He called violence a man's choice.
